title: “MY SHEEP HEAR MY VOICE” — BUT WHAT IF THE VOICE YOU’VE BEEN FOLLOWING ISN’T JESUS?
paragraphs: “MY SHEEP HEAR MY VOICE” — BUT WHAT IF THE VOICE YOU’VE BEEN FOLLOWING ISN’T JESUS?

One of the most quoted promises in John 10:27 may also be one of the most misunderstood. What Jesus actually meant could change the way you understand faith, discernment, obedience, and your relationship with God forever.
What if the most dangerous voice in your life is not the one telling you to abandon God, but the one convincing you that you are following Him when you are actually following yourself?
Think about that for a moment.
How many times have we said, “God told me,” when what we really meant was, “This is what I wanted”?
How many relationships have we entered because we believed God sent someone, only to discover that loneliness was doing the talking?
How many decisions have we justified with spiritual language because admitting that we were wrong would have wounded our pride?
How many times have we mistaken emotional excitement for divine confirmation, personal ambition for God's calling, and the silence of our conscience for the peace of the Holy Spirit?
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question of all:
Have we become so familiar with talking about Jesus that we have forgotten what it means to actually follow Him?
Jesus said something in John 10:27 that should bring extraordinary comfort to the believer, but also profound conviction to anyone who claims to belong to Him.
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” — John 10:27, KJV
Many Christians quote the first part of that verse.
Far fewer seriously examine the last.
We want to hear His voice.
We want supernatural confirmation.
We want direction, reassurance, prophetic words, answered prayers, and unmistakable signs that God is moving in our lives.
But Jesus did not merely say that His sheep hear Him.
He said they follow Him.
And there is an enormous difference between wanting to hear what God has to say and being willing to obey what He has already said.
To understand the depth of this statement, we need to examine the Greek text in which the Gospel of John was preserved:
Τὰ πρόβατα τὰ ἐμὰ τῆς φωνῆς μου ἀκούουσιν, κἀγὼ γινώσκω αὐτά, καὶ ἀκολουθοῦσίν μοι.
Ta probata ta ema tēs phōnēs mou akouousin, kagō ginōskō auta, kai akolouthousin moi.
A close English translation reads:
“The sheep that are mine hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.”

Jesus likely spoke Aramaic in many of His earthly conversations, but the canonical Gospel of John comes to us in Koine Greek. Therefore, the Greek text is the appropriate foundation for examining the wording of this passage rather than claiming certainty about an unrecoverable original Aramaic utterance.
The Greek word translated as “hear” is ἀκούουσιν (akouousin), from ἀκούω (akouō), meaning to hear or listen.

The word itself does not automatically mean obedience in every context. However, Jesus connects hearing with following, making it clear that He is describing something deeper than merely receiving audible information.
The sheep recognize and respond to their Shepherd.
They do not simply hear a sound.
They respond to a Person.
This echoes an important biblical pattern found in the Hebrew Scriptures.
In Deuteronomy 6:4, Israel is called to listen:
שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ יְהוָה אֶחָד
Shema Yisrael, Adonai Eloheinu, Adonai Echad.
“Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD.” — Deuteronomy 6:4, KJV
The Hebrew word שָׁמַע (shama) can mean hearing, listening, heeding, or obeying, depending on its context.
Throughout Scripture, truly listening to God is frequently connected with responding faithfully to Him.
The issue is not whether sound reaches our ears.
The issue is whether God's truth reaches our hearts and changes the direction of our lives.
Imagine a man sitting alone in his car after another argument with his wife.
His hands are gripping the steering wheel. His eyes are exhausted. He knows the words he said were cruel, but he keeps replaying everything she did wrong.
He opens his phone, scrolls through Christian videos, and eventually finds a message about how God removes people who disturb your peace.
Suddenly, he feels justified.
Maybe God is telling him to walk away.
Maybe his wife is the problem.
Maybe he deserves better.
But somewhere beneath all the noise, Scripture confronts him with something he does not want to hear.
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.” — Ephesians 5:25, KJV
He wanted confirmation.
Scripture confronted him with responsibility.
He wanted permission to protect his pride.
Christ called him toward humility, love, and repentance.
Which message was more comfortable?
And which was more consistent with the Shepherd?

This does not mean someone must remain in an abusive or dangerous situation. Seeking safety and appropriate help is not a failure of Christian faith. But in ordinary conflicts, we must be careful not to use spiritual language to escape the accountability Scripture places upon us.
Sometimes the truth we least want to hear is the very truth we most desperately need.
The context of John 10 makes Jesus' words even more powerful.
He was not giving His disciples a technique for receiving secret messages from heaven.
He was revealing His identity as the Good Shepherd.

The conversation follows the events of John 9, where Jesus healed a man who had been blind from birth. Instead of celebrating God's work, certain religious authorities interrogated the man and eventually cast him out.
Imagine being rejected by the very people you expected to represent God.
Imagine receiving a miracle and losing your community.
Imagine finally being able to see the world around you, only to discover how spiritually blind some of the people around you had become.
But John 9:35 records something beautiful.
Jesus heard that the man had been cast out.
And Jesus found him.
The religious authorities had rejected him.
The Shepherd went looking for him.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
That is the difference between spiritual leadership that protects its own power and the Shepherd who gives Himself for His sheep.

It also echoes Ezekiel 34, where God condemns Israel's unfaithful shepherds for feeding themselves while neglecting the flock. God promises to seek the lost, care for the injured, and shepherd His people, including through the promised Davidic shepherd.
When Jesus declares Himself the Good Shepherd in John 10, He stands within this extraordinary biblical promise.
“I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.” — John 10:11, KJV
He is not merely another religious teacher offering advice.
He is the Shepherd who lays down His life to save His flock.
Later, during the Feast of Dedication, Jesus is confronted by people demanding that He tell them plainly whether He is the Christ.
Jesus points to His works and addresses their unbelief in John 10:24–26.
Then comes the declaration:
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.”
The immediate context is about recognizing Jesus, believing in Him, belonging to Him, and receiving eternal life through Him.
It is not primarily a promise that every Christian will receive an audible voice, a private revelation, a dream, or supernatural instructions concerning every decision.
That distinction matters.
Because somewhere tonight, a sincere believer may be lying awake wondering why God never speaks to them the way other Christians claim He speaks to them.
They have prayed.
They have cried.
They have fasted.
They have waited.
They have watched people announce, “God told me this,” and “God showed me that,” until they began wondering whether something was wrong with their own faith.
Maybe that person is you.
You love Jesus, but you do not always feel His presence.
You read your Bible, but sometimes the words seem difficult to understand.
You pray, but the room remains quiet.
You wonder whether the Shepherd has forgotten your name.
Please understand what Jesus actually promised.
The absence of an extraordinary spiritual experience is not evidence that you do not belong to Christ.
Scripture records occasions when God communicated through dreams, visions, and extraordinary revelations. But John 10:27 does not establish such experiences as the required evidence of salvation.

Christians differ on how certain spiritual gifts and forms of divine guidance operate today. Nevertheless, every claim of divine guidance must be tested, and no subjective impression possesses authority to overturn God's revealed truth.
The apostle Paul reminds us in 2 Timothy 3:16–17 that Scripture is God-breathed and equips God's people for every good work.
Hebrews 1:1–2 declares that God has spoken climactically through His Son.
And 1 John 4:1 warns believers not to believe every spirit but to test them.
You do not need to manufacture a supernatural experience to prove that Jesus loves you.
You do not need to compete with someone else's testimony.
You do not need to hear an audible whisper before trusting the promises He has already given.
Your feelings may fluctuate.
His faithfulness does not.
Your emotions may become exhausted.
His Word remains true.
Your prayers may sometimes feel painfully unanswered.
But your emotional experience is not the final authority on whether Christ has abandoned you.
Notice the next expression in John 10:27.
κἀγὼ γινώσκω αὐτά — kagō ginōskō auta.
“And I know them.”
The Greek verb γινώσκω (ginōskō) means to know, recognize, or understand. In this context, Jesus is describing His personal relationship with those who belong to Him.
He does not merely know that they exist.
They are His sheep.
The Shepherd knows His flock.
He knows the battles you cannot explain.
He knows the prayers you could barely finish.
He knows the shame you carry behind your carefully maintained appearance.
He knows the history you are afraid someone will discover.
He knows the moments when your faith felt strong and the nights when you wondered whether you had any faith left.
And the wonder of the Gospel is not that you successfully concealed your brokenness from Jesus.
It is that He knew the truth about sinners and willingly went to the cross to redeem them.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we became respectable.
Not after we repaired our reputations.
Not after we finally learned how to appear spiritual.
While we were still sinners.
That is grace.
But grace must never be confused with permission to continue embracing the sin from which Christ came to redeem us.
Jesus completes His statement with these words:
καὶ ἀκολουθοῦσίν μοι — kai akolouthousin moi.
“And they follow me.”
The Greek verb ἀκολουθέω (akoloutheō) means to follow, accompany, or go after someone. In the Gospels, it frequently describes discipleship.
The verbs for hearing, knowing, and following in this passage are in the present tense, presenting these realities as characteristic of the relationship between the Shepherd and His sheep.
Jesus is describing a life oriented toward Him.
Not sinless perfection.
Not uninterrupted spiritual success.
Not salvation earned through religious performance.
But genuine discipleship.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by our works, as Ephesians 2:8–9 makes unmistakably clear. Yet the very next verse explains that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Obedience is not the purchase price of salvation.
It is the fruit of a life being transformed by grace.
A sheep can stumble.
A believer can struggle.
A disciple can experience fear, confusion, temptation, and even devastating failure.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
The same Peter who had confidently declared his loyalty eventually found himself weeping bitterly over his own betrayal.
His failure was public enough to become part of the biblical record.
Imagine carrying that memory.
Imagine knowing that when your Savior was suffering, you insisted you did not even know Him.
Yet the resurrected Jesus restored Peter in John 21.
And what did Jesus say to him?
The scandal of Peter's failure was not the final chapter of his story.
Jesus called him forward.
That is why the Gospel is not merely a message for people who have never fallen.
It is good news for people who have fallen and discovered that their only hope is the mercy of Christ.
From denial to restoration.
From shame to renewed discipleship.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But we must also confront an uncomfortable reality.
There is a difference between struggling against sin and deliberately using grace to defend it.
There is a difference between falling while following Christ and refusing to follow Him because we prefer our own direction.
There is a difference between confessing our weakness and celebrating our rebellion.
When Jesus calls us to forgive, we cannot automatically declare our bitterness a divine instruction.
When Scripture calls us toward sexual holiness, we cannot assume that the intensity of our desires makes them God's approval.
When the Gospel confronts our dishonesty, greed, arrogance, prejudice, or hypocrisy, we cannot silence its conviction by finding a preacher who tells us what we would rather hear.
Paul warned Timothy about people gathering teachers to satisfy their own desires in 2 Timothy 4:3–4.
The human heart has an extraordinary ability to turn its preferences into theology.
And that is precisely why discernment matters.
Not every thought that enters your mind is from God.
Not every dream is a divine revelation.
Not every opportunity is an open door you are required to enter.
Not every coincidence is a prophetic sign.
Not every peaceful feeling confirms that your decision is right.
And not every uncomfortable conviction is an attack from the enemy.
Sometimes obedience is uncomfortable because it requires surrendering something we have spent years protecting.
Jesus Himself said in Luke 9:23:
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.”
The Shepherd does not always lead us toward convenience.
He leads us toward Himself.
So when you believe God is directing you, examine that impression carefully.
Does it agree with Scripture?
Does it reflect the character and teaching of Jesus?
Does it encourage truth, holiness, humility, love, and faithfulness?
Are you willing to receive correction from mature believers?
Would you still obey God's revealed Word if it contradicted the answer you desperately wanted?
James 3:17 describes wisdom from above as pure, peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere.
Biblical discernment is not about becoming suspicious of everything.
It is about becoming so grounded in Christ that deception does not easily carry you away.
And when you discover that you have been wrong, repentance is not humiliation without hope.
It is an invitation to return.
Perhaps this article has uncovered something you have been avoiding.
Perhaps you have been asking God for another sign when you already know what Scripture requires.
Perhaps you have been waiting for a supernatural confirmation before apologizing to someone you wounded.
Perhaps you have been calling your resentment discernment, your pride conviction, or your unwillingness to change spiritual maturity.
Or perhaps you are simply exhausted from trying to hear God through the noise of fear, disappointment, and unanswered questions.
Whatever brought you here, you can respond to Christ today.
You do not have to pretend.
You do not have to perform.
You can pray:

Lord Jesus, forgive me for the times I confused my desires with Your direction. Forgive me for seeking confirmation instead of surrender. Teach me to recognize Your truth through Scripture, to test what I believe, and to follow You even when obedience costs me something. Restore what sin has damaged in me. Give me a humble and teachable heart. When I wander, correct me. When I fall, lead me toward repentance. When I am afraid, remind me of Your promises. Let my life belong to You, not merely my words. Amen.
You do not need to disclose your private struggles publicly. God already knows them. But your willingness to ask for prayer may remind another struggling believer that they are not alone.
And before you leave, read what Jesus says immediately after John 10:27.
“And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand.” — John 10:28, KJV
Do you see the beauty of that promise?
The Shepherd does not merely call His sheep.
He gives them eternal life.
The foundation of their hope is not the strength of their emotions, the perfection of their performance, or their ability to decipher every spiritual impression.
It is the saving power and faithfulness of Jesus Christ.
The hands that hold His sheep are the hands that were wounded for sinners.
The Shepherd who calls us to follow Him is the Shepherd who laid down His life and rose again.
Our ultimate confidence rests in Him.
Someone may be following destructive advice disguised as spiritual wisdom. Someone may have become convinced that God has abandoned them simply because they cannot feel His presence.
You may never know who needed to read these words.
But making biblical truth available to others is a meaningful way to serve them.
Ministry requires time, dedication, resources, and the faithful support of people who believe in making the Gospel accessible to others.
You may prayerfully choose to make this support part of your voluntary Christian giving and offerings, alongside your responsibilities to your local church, family, and those in need.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should come from a willing heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Jesus has already paid the price of our redemption.
But together, we can help make Christ-centered resources available to more people.
We want you to know Jesus more than we want anything from you.

Because when all the noise finally disappears, when the opinions of people no longer matter, when the applause fades and the world can offer you nothing more, the question will not be how many extraordinary spiritual experiences you collected.
It will not be how many times you claimed God spoke to you.
It will not be how religious you appeared to everyone around you.
What matters is whether you belong to Jesus Christ.
Whether your hope rests in His finished work.
Whether the Shepherd you profess with your lips is the Shepherd you trust with your life.
You may have wandered farther than you ever intended.
You may have followed voices that promised freedom but left you in chains.
You may have confused your own desires with God's direction.
But do not allow yesterday's rebellion to become today's excuse for remaining distant from Christ.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Return to His Word.
Trust His mercy.
Follow the Shepherd.
There is forgiveness for the repentant sinner. There is hope for the broken disciple. There is grace for those who come to Christ in faith.
The world has enough voices telling you what you want to hear.
You need the Shepherd who loves you enough to tell you the truth.
The greatest tragedy is not that you spent years searching for God's voice. It is that Jesus was calling you to follow Him while you were waiting for Him to agree with you.
